sections.h2: How can a Fairfield, Ohio homeowner sell quickly?
sections.html:
Three paths exist for Fairfield owners: hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or accept a cash purchase. The deciding factors are the house's condition and your closing date. Fairfield has the highest home values of the four cities covered in this series, which makes a well kept house a strong candidate for a conventional listing.

  • Agent listing: strongest for updated houses, especially ones inside the Fairfield City School District.
  • By owner: keeps the commission, but you handle disclosure paperwork and every showing.
  • Cash buyer: suits an outdated or damaged house, an estate, or a seller who needs to leave town fast.

Where the sale falls under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, you give buyers a signed disclosure form. The statute exempts transfers to a buyer who has lived in the home as a personal residence for at least a year, and transfers to a spouse or to a lineal relative, so a sale to a tenant or family member may skip it.

sections.h2: Where is Fairfield and how did it grow?
sections.html:
Fairfield is a city in southern Butler County, about 25 miles north of Cincinnati, on the east bank of the Great Miami River. It formed in 1955 from part of Fairfield Township and absorbed the old hamlets of Symmes Corner, Fair Play, Furmandale and Stockton. Symmes Corner, at Pleasant Avenue and Nilles Road, is now the town center. Fair Play, on the river's east bank, was known for Ohio's first paper mill before a flood in the late 1800s destroyed it. Stockton began as Jones Station on the rail line, and Furmandale, at Winton and Nilles roads, was nicknamed Snaptown. The Miami and Erie Canal ran a few miles east and carried farm goods before the railroad arrived.

The land belonged to the Symmes Purchase of 1788. The Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton Railway, now CSX, came through in the 1850s, and a rail line still bisects the city. Farming dominated until the mid twentieth century, when Hamilton's industry spread south and Fisher Body built a plant at State Route 4 and Symmes Road. The village passed 5,000 residents by 1960 and became a statutory city, and the Interstate 275 beltway in the late 1970s brought commuters from north of Cincinnati.

Most of the city sits above the Great Miami Buried Valley Aquifer, which supplies drinking water to Fairfield, Hamilton and Cincinnati. The city's boundaries reach Hamilton on the north, West Chester on the east and Springdale and Forest Park on the south, and a small part crosses into Hamilton County with no residents. Public transit comes from the Butler County Regional Transit Authority and the Southwest Ohio Regional Transit Authority.

sections.h2: Who are the biggest employers around Fairfield homes?
sections.html:
Fairfield's economy is diversified, with no single industry on top, and two of its leading employers are insurance companies. The city's list of employers drives buyer demand for nearby houses.

Cincinnati Financial has its corporate headquarters here, and Jungle Jim's International Market, which began as a produce stand in 1971, draws shoppers from across the region. The Fairfield City School District runs Fairfield High School, the Fairfield Freshmen School, two middle schools and six elementary schools, and parochial options include Sacred Heart of Jesus School, Stephen T. Badin High School and Cincinnati Christian schools. A Miami University branch campus sits a few miles north in Hamilton, and the Fairfield Lane Library belongs to the Lane Public Library system.

sections.h2: How expensive is Fairfield housing compared with its neighbors?
sections.html:
Fairfield's owner occupied homes carry a 2020 to 2024 median value of $234,500 in Census Bureau QuickFacts, and owners live in 63.2 percent of the city's houses, both the highest among the four cities in this series. The July 2025 population estimate is 44,682, a 0.5 percent dip against the 2020 base and above the 42,510 counted in 2010.

  • Median gross rent: $1,242
  • Households: 18,428, averaging 2.41 people
  • Median household income: $77,937
  • Per capita income: $40,668
  • College graduates among adults 25 and older: 30.7 percent
  • Persons in poverty: 8.4 percent
  • Foreign born residents: 12.0 percent
  • Average commute: 23.8 minutes

The 2020 census counted 44,907 residents across 21.06 square miles, standing about 646 feet above sea level. Mail uses ZIP code 45014, with small areas in 45011 and 45069, under area code 513.

sections.h2: What city projects and codes affect a Fairfield sale?
sections.html:
The Development Services Department handles building and site plan reviews, building permits and inspections, planning, economic development and property maintenance inspections. Its number is (513) 867-5345. Ask there about permits that were opened but never closed, because unfinished work on a deck, finished basement or addition can surface during a buyer's inspection.

Two projects shape how buyers talk about the city. The Federal Railroad Administration awarded $40 million toward the Symmes Road Grade Separation Project, a total investment of about $50 million at a crossing of the rail line. Separately, Fairfield is updating its 2019 comprehensive plan, Fairfield Forward, with attention to redevelopment along Route 4 and in the Town Center.

Development Services also runs property maintenance inspections, so a violation tied to your address, such as a vacant or neglected lot next door, falls to the same office.

sections.h2: How does the Butler County Auditor transfer a deed for a Fairfield house?
sections.html:
Fairfield sits in Butler County, so the Butler County Auditor's Conveyance Department processes the transfer and collects the fees. Standards under Ohio Revised Code 319.203 bar the Auditor from transferring any conveyance that does not meet them.

  • The conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the next hundred, plus $0.50 per parcel.
  • Fees are accepted by cash or check only, and checks are payable to the Butler County Auditor.
  • The DTE Form 100 or 100EX must be complete, with a valid legal description attached to the deed.
  • Contact the Engineer's Office at 513-867-5744 to have the legal description pre-approved before you submit.

The Recorder's Office holds the recorded deed, and its number is 513-887-3196. The Auditor's records start in 1993, and the Recorder's electronic records reach back to 1987. The Recorder also offers a free fraud alert service called Fraudsleuth that emails you when a document is recorded under your name, which is worth joining before you list. Deeds older than 1987 may require a visit to the Recorder's office to search the paper books, so start early if a title question could delay your closing.

faqs.q: What does the Butler County Auditor charge for a deed transfer?
faqs.a: The Auditor lists a conveyance fee of $3.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the next hundred, plus $0.50 per parcel. Payment is by cash or check only.

faqs.q: Who approves the legal description on a Fairfield deed?
faqs.a: The Butler County Engineer's Office pre-approves it. Call 513-867-5744 before you submit the deed, since the Auditor requires a valid legal description.

faqs.q: Where do I report a vacant or neglected house in Fairfield?
faqs.a: Contact the Development Services Department at (513) 867-5345, which handles property maintenance inspections for the city.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a disclosure form if I sell to my own child in Fairfield?
faqs.a: Probably not. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 exempts transfers to a spouse or to a person in a direct line of descent. Confirm the details with the attorney or title company handling the deed.

faqs.q: What is the median value of a Fairfield home?
faqs.a: Census data for 2020 to 2024 shows $234,500 as the median for owner occupied homes in Fairfield, the highest among Elyria, Euclid, Fairborn and Fairfield. Your own price depends on condition, floor plan and street, so compare recent sales within a few blocks.
